changes.before: Create a generic collection that preserves the item type for both numbers and text.
changes.after: Use one collection class while keeping each collection's item type.

before: A generic lets one piece of code work with different types while remembering which type was chosen. The type parameter T is a placeholder for a type, not a runtime value. Collection<number> chooses number; Collection<string> chooses string. Both can use the same storage and methods, while TypeScript checks which values can go into each instance.

private asks TypeScript to prevent outside code from directly using values; callers use the methods. This TypeScript private keyword is not a security boundary for secret data at runtime. void means add does not promise a useful returned value. first returns T | undefined because an empty array has no first item. undefined means absent, rather than the number zero or an empty string.

The same methods keep their chosen return types: counts.first() is number | undefined, while colors.first() is string | undefined. Replacing T with any would lose that connection and hide wrong-type mistakes. A bare new Collection() can still represent an empty collection, but an explicit type parameter is clearer when choosing the values you plan to store.

For the exercise, add must push into this.values, and first must return this.values[0]. Set firstNumber from numbers.first() and firstWord from words.first(). With the supplied inputs those values are 7 and maple. Adding does not replace the earlier item, so the first value stays first after later additions. Do not invent a default when the collection is empty.

After the valid solution compiles, temporarily try numbers.add('seven'). Expect a compiler error, then remove that call. A generic class provides compile-time consistency; it does not inspect unknown network values by itself. Check untrusted values before calling add. Distinguishing an empty collection from one containing 0 or empty text is part of preserving the actual stored value.
after: A generic class can be used with different types. `T` stands for the chosen type. A Shelf<number> stores numbers; a Shelf<string> stores text. Each uses the same class code.

Private tells TypeScript that outside code should use the methods instead of accessing values directly. Void means add promises no useful result. First returns T or undefined because the array might be empty.
An empty shelf returns undefined. Check `value !== undefined` before using a possible result. This check still accepts a stored 0 or an empty string.
A number shelf's first result is number or undefined. A text shelf's first result is string or undefined. Keeping T preserves that connection; using any would lose it.

For Collection, push each new value into `this.values`. Return `this.values[0]` from first. The supplied number and text collections should give 7 and maple. Leave an empty collection's result as undefined.
Adding text to a number collection causes a type error. TypeScript private and generic types are checking rules, not protection for secrets or checks of outside data while the program runs.

before: Define Collection<T> with an array inside it to store its values.
Add an add method to store a value and a first method to return the first value.
Add 7 to a Collection<number>. Save the result of first() as firstNumber.
Add "maple" to a Collection<string>. Save the result of first() as firstWord.
Check that first() returns undefined for an empty Collection<boolean>.
after: Store items in a T array inside Collection.
Make add append an item and first read position 0.
Save the number collection's first result as firstNumber.
Save the text collection's first result as firstWord.
Check an empty collection and run the checks.

before: Use `push` to keep the supplied value.
Return `this.values[0]`; its type includes undefined because a collection may be empty.
after: Push adds at the end without replacing earlier items.
Return the actual first item, including undefined when the list is empty.

before.question: words is a Collection<string>. Which call keeps its chosen element type?
before.explanation: The type parameter string requires text inputs. Quoted "12" is text even though its characters are digits. The unquoted number and the Boolean do not meet that type.

after.question: Words is a Collection<string>. Which item can it accept?
after.explanation: This collection accepts text. Quotes make "12" a text value.

changes.before: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: numbers.add("seven"); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.
changes.after: To try a type error, temporarily add text to the number collection. Read the error, then remove the invalid call.

project.title: A reusable typed collection
project.task: Make one generic collection class work for numbers and text while preserving each item type.
project.done_when: Items stay in order, first returns the actual first item or undefined, wrong item types are rejected, and the checks pass.
